n: The tour of the wall begins at the northeast, near the temple, and moves counterclockwise around the city. Fittingly, the high priest and priests start the work and dedicate their section to God.

f.g: Near the temple, where sheep for sacrifice were likely brought in; compare the pool by the sheep market in John 5:2.
Dedicated it to the Lord as holy.
Means “Hundred” — perhaps the Tower of the Hundred.

n: Men from Jericho, about 15 miles away, help build. People from towns all over Judah came to work on the capital’s wall.
The Fish Gate on the north side was probably where fishermen from Tyre and Galilee brought their catch to market. This family rebuilt it completely, beams to locks.

f.g: Heavy bolts placed across gates to lock them.

n: Meremoth, the priest who had received Ezra’s treasure, repairs here — and he will repair a second section later (verse 21). Some workers did double duty.
The ordinary people of Tekoa work hard, but their nobles refuse to bend their necks to the labor. It is the one sour note in the list — pride kept some from serving.

f.g: People of Tekoa, a town south of Bethlehem and home of the prophet Amos (Amos 1:1).

f.w: put not their necks to the work
f.g: Like an ox refusing the yoke — unwilling to serve.

n: Two men rebuild the “Old Gate,” probably at the northwest corner of the city.

f.g: Perhaps “the gate of the old city”; some translate it “Jeshanah Gate.”

n: Men from Gibeon and Mizpah, towns north of Jerusalem, repair the next section, up to the residence used by the provincial governor.

f.w: the throne of the governor on this side the river
f.g: Probably the official seat or quarters of the Persian governor west of the Euphrates.

n: Skilled craftsmen — a goldsmith and a perfume maker — lay down their delicate trades to do rough stonework. They restore the wall as far as the “Broad Wall.”

f.g: Perfume or ointment makers.
A thick section of wall; archaeologists have found a massive wall in Jerusalem from Hezekiah’s time often linked to it.

n: Rephaiah, governor of half of the Jerusalem district, works alongside the common people. Leaders served with their own hands.

f.w: the ruler of the half part of Jerusalem
f.g: Head of one of two administrative halves of the Jerusalem district.

n: Jedaiah repairs the stretch right in front of his own house. Working near home made sense — each family protected what it loved most.

f.g: Opposite or in front of his house.

n: These two men rebuild “the other piece,” suggesting this was their second assignment, along with the Tower of the Ovens, where bread may have been baked.

f.g: The Tower of the Ovens, perhaps near the bakers’ street (Jeremiah 37:21).

n: A district ruler named Shallum works with his daughters — a lovely detail showing that women also took part in rebuilding the wall.

f.g: The only women mentioned among the builders.

n: The people of Zanoah rebuild the Valley Gate and repair about a third of a mile of wall to the Dung Gate. The long stretch may mean this part was less damaged.

f.g: About 1,500 feet (450 meters); a cubit was about 18 inches.

n: A district ruler from Beth-haccerem rebuilds the Dung Gate, through which refuse was taken out of the city.
The Fountain Gate and the wall by the Pool of Siloam are rebuilt, near the stairs leading down from the oldest part of Jerusalem, the City of David.

f.g: The Pool of Siloam, fed by Hezekiah’s tunnel; compare John 9:7.
The original hill of Jerusalem that David captured (2 Samuel 5:7).

n: Another man named Nehemiah (not the governor) repairs the area across from King David’s tombs, near a reservoir and the old barracks of David’s warriors.

f.g: Probably barracks for the king’s elite soldiers (2 Samuel 23:8).

n: Levites join the work, along with a ruler from Keilah, a town southwest of Jerusalem.
The other half of the Keilah district is represented by its ruler, Bavai. Both halves of the district contributed.
Ezer, ruler of Mizpah, repairs a section near the armory, where the wall turns a corner.

f.g: A storehouse for weapons.

n: Baruch is the only builder described as working “earnestly” — eagerly, with fire. His section reaches the high priest’s house.

f.g: With zeal or burning energy; the only worker singled out this way.

n: Meremoth takes on his second section, the length of the high priest’s large house.
Priests from the surrounding countryside, probably the Jordan Valley region, do their share.

f.g: Men of the surrounding region, likely the Jordan Valley.

n: More men repair the wall beside their own homes. When everyone strengthens the part closest to them, the whole city becomes secure.
Binnui repairs from Azariah’s house to the corner where the wall bends.

f.g: A corner or angle where the wall changes direction.

n: This section runs past a tower projecting from the old royal palace near the prison courtyard — the area where Jeremiah was once held.

f.g: The upper palace of the former kings of Judah.

n: The temple servants lived on Ophel, the hill between the temple and the City of David, near the Water Gate on the east. The Water Gate later becomes the place where Ezra reads the law.

f.g: Means “swelling” or “hill” — the ridge just south of the temple mount.

n: The people of Tekoa do a second section, even though their nobles refused to help (verse 5). The common people made up for their leaders’ pride.
Priests repair near the Horse Gate, each one in front of his own house.
A priest and the keeper of the East Gate repair next. Each gate had its own guardians.

f.g: A gate facing east toward the Mount of Olives.

n: Meshullam repairs in front of his own room. Sadly, his family later formed a marriage alliance with Nehemiah’s enemy Tobiah.

f.g: A room or dwelling.

n: Malchiah, son of a goldsmith, works near the quarters of temple servants and merchants, close to the Inspection Gate.

f.g: Means “muster” or “inspection” — the Inspection Gate, perhaps where people or goods were counted.

n: Goldsmiths and merchants close the circle, finishing back at the Sheep Gate where the high priest began. The whole wall was rebuilt by a united people, each doing a part.
